report:
## Summary

The claim has moderate support, but it's more nuanced than a simple "yes."

**Strongest evidence:** A systematic review and meta-analysis by Kappelmann et al. (Molecular Psychiatry, 2018) pooled randomized trials of anti-cytokine drugs (TNF inhibitors, IL-6 blockers, etc.) given for chronic inflammatory diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis, where depressive symptoms were tracked as a secondary outcome. They found a significant overall antidepressant effect compared to placebo, independent of the drugs' effects on the underlying physical disease—suggesting cytokines may play a causal role in depression, not just correlate with it (https://www.nature.com/articles/mp2016167; summarized in press coverage such as https://www.newscientist.com/article/2109382-anti-inflammatory-drugs-can-relieve-symptoms-of-depression/).

**Important caveat—effects don't generalize to primary depression:** When TNF antagonists have been tested directly as antidepressants in people with treatment-resistant major depression (not inflammatory disease), results are mixed. Raison et al.'s RCT of infliximab found no overall benefit versus placebo, though a subgroup with elevated baseline inflammatory markers (CRP) did respond better (https://chm-web.files.svdcdn.com/production/files-publications/Raison-A-Randomized-Controlled-Trial-of-the-Tumor-Necrosis-Factor-Antagonist-Infliximab-for-Treatment-Resistant-Depression.pdf). A more recent 2024 trial similarly found TNF-antagonism improved motivational deficits only in depressed patients selected for high inflammation (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41380-024-02751-x).

**Conclusion:** The evidence supports the claim specifically for people with chronic inflammatory conditions (arthritis, psoriasis, etc.)—anti-cytokine drugs do appear to reduce co-occurring depressive symptoms, likely via reducing systemic inflammation. However, this benefit doesn't clearly extend to unselected depression patients without inflammatory disease, and effects are strongest when baseline inflammation markers are elevated. The claim is reasonably well-supported but context-dependent.
